title: Prevalence and Actionability of MTAP Loss in Driver Oncogene-Positive and Oncogene-Negative Lung Cancer.
authors: Sakai T, Piotrowska Z, Wang CI et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: MTAP loss co-occurs with actionable genomic alterations in NSCLC and creates vulnerability to protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) inhibition. Estimates of prevalence of MTAP loss rely on next-generation sequencing which can underestimate copy losses. Moreover, the activity of PRMT5 inhibitors in oncogene-driven NSCLC is not well established.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We assessed MTAP expression by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in 243 NSCLCs (n=132 early stage, n=111 metastatic), including 33 specimens with paired lymph nodes. Activity of PRMT5 inhibitor monotherapy and in combination with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) was evaluated in MTAP-deleted NSCLC cell lines harboring EGFR or KRAS mutations or ALK rearrangements.
RESULTS: Among 243 NSCLC specimens from 240 patients (72% with driver alterations, 90% adenocarcinoma), MTAP loss was identified in 42 (17%) specimens, including 17 (13%) early-stage and 22 (20%) metastatic specimens. MTAP loss occurred in 24% of stage 4 driver-positive NSCLCs versus 14% of driver-negative tumors (p=0.314). Twenty-one (64%) lung-nodal pairs demonstrated concordance; eight cases only exhibited decreased MTAP expression in nodes. Variable sensitivity to PRMT5 inhibitors was observed in 22 MTAP-deleted NSCLC cell lines (9 EGFR-mutant, 7 KRAS-mutant, 6 ALK-rearranged), with responses seen in TKI-sensitive and TKI-resistant lines. SDMA (symmetric dimethylarginine) expression did not predict PRMT5 inhibitor sensitivity. TKI + PRMT5 inhibitor combos had greater activity than monotherapy.
CONCLUSIONS: MTAP loss occurs in 17% of NSCLC, including 24% of oncogene-driven tumors. PRMT5 inhibitor activity is independent of TKI exposure and SDMA expression and enhanced by TKI therapy. These findings support evaluation of PRMT5 inhibitor + TKIs in oncogene-driven NSCLC.

title: The genomic landscape of non-small cell lung cancer in Northern Ireland: A regional retrospective cross-sectional study.
authors: Brown R, Abladey A, Crean C et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for ~ 85% of lung cancer cases and has a diverse molecular profile. Incorporation of next generation sequencing into routine testing has revolutionised NSCLC care, allowing improved access to targeted therapies.
AIMS: In this study, we have assessed the molecular profile of NSCLC patients in Northern Ireland. Additionally, we evaluated associations between molecular profiles and clinicopathologic variables including age, sex, PD-L1 status and histologic subtype.
METHODS: DNA was extracted from formalin fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue from patients sent for next generation sequencing (NGS) testing between October 2022 and December 2024. Sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq 6000 Illumina platform using the NovaSeq SP 50bp paired-end kit. Patient demographics and clinicopathological information were collected by retrospective review of the patients' electronic care records and PD-L1 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry.
RESULTS: NGS analysis identified actionable variants in 650 (51%) patients. The most commonly mutated genes were KRAS (30.5%), EGFR (10.5%), BRAF (3.9%) and MET (2.3%). Assessment of clinicopathological features showed enrichment for younger age in ALK-positive vs ALK-wild type tumours and low PD-L1 positivity in EGFR-positive tumours.
CONCLUSIONS: The implementation of NGS as part of the routine diagnostic service has improved our understanding of the molecular landscape of NSCLC in Northern Ireland and significantly expanded the application of precision medicine to a larger number of NSCLC patients within the region.

title: Thiophen-2-ylsulfonyl indole-3-carbaldehyde thiosemicarbazones as selective prostate cancer agents: biological profiling and molecular targeting studies.
authors: Batool K, İnce Hİ, Şenol AM et al.
abstract: A series of thiophen-2-ylsulfonyl indole-3-carbaldehyde thiosemicarbazone derivatives 5a-5t was synthesized and evaluated for anticancer activity using biological and computational methods. The cytotoxic activity of these compounds was tested on A549, LNCaP, and HUVEC cell lines utilizing the MTT assay, with sorafenib used as a control drug. The activity of the derivatives was shown to be cell line- and substituent-dependent, with the highest cytotoxicity against LNCaP cells. Compound 5d, bearing a 2,3-dichlorophenyl group, was the most potent derivative against LNCaP cells (IC50 = 2.50 µM; SI = 33.7), while compounds 5b and 5c also showed notable activity (IC50 = 7.96 and 5.30 µM, respectively). These synthesized compounds showed preferential activity towards prostate cancer (LNCaP) cells specifically in comparison with lung cancer A549 cells. Thus, subsequent computational studies were directed to the molecular targets associated with prostate cancer. The docking study of compounds 5b-5d against AR, EGFR, VEGFR-2, AKT1, mTOR, and PI3Kα, followed by MM-GBSA analysis, indicated their good binding activity with particular reference to the AR target. An MD simulation of 250 ns on the AR-compound 5d complex confirmed the stability and constant interaction with important residues. ADME and DFT analyses determined the properties of the selected compounds. Overall, compound 5d emerged as a promising lead for further investigation against prostate cancer. Our data provide a foundation for the rational design and optimization of thiosemicarbazone-based anticancer agents and advance research into their molecular mechanisms, target selectivity, and preclinical therapeutic potential.

title: Prolonged survival after small-cell transformation of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma: a case report.
authors: Yan Y, Du D, Wen F et al.
abstract: Transformed small cell lung cancer (T-SCLC) is most commonly observed in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and represents an important mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). Its reported clinical incidence is approximately 3%-10%. Patients with T-SCLC often experience rapid disease progression and poor overall prognosis, and no established standard treatment regimen is currently available. We report a case of advanced EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with RB1, TP53, and BRCA2 co-mutations that underwent small-cell transformation during treatment. Small-cell transformation was detected through close surveillance and confirmed by repeat biopsy. The patient subsequently received individualized multimodal therapy, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and local radiotherapy, and remained alive 43 months after the initial diagnosis.

title: Primary resistance to afatinib in a patient with NSCLC harboring EGFR p.E709_T710delinsD and brain metastases: a case report and literature review.
authors: Dong SS, Zhang X, Dong W
abstract: EGFR p.E709_T710delinsD is a rare in-frame deletion-insertion P-loop and alpha-C-helix compressing (PACC) mutation of EGFR exon 18. Current evidence suggests that patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring this variant generally respond to afatinib. However, primary resistance to afatinib in this molecular subset is rarely reported. We report a 68-year-old man diagnosed with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma harboring an EGFR p.E709_T710delinsD mutation (variant allele frequency, 45.9%) with co-occurring EGFR amplification (fold change 1.5). Brain metastases were present at baseline. The patient was treated with oral afatinib at an initial dose of 30 mg once daily but the disease progressed rapidly, suggesting possible primary targeted resistance. The patient died 5 weeks later. This case represents a rare example of primary resistance to afatinib in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring the EGFR p.E709_T710delinsD mutation. Given the lack of tissue and molecular evidence to confirm the resistance mechanism in this case, this report combines previous literature to explore the potential factors associated with treatment failure and their clinical implications. This case does not refute the overall sensitivity of this variant to afatinib, but suggests that in patients with high baseline disease burden and aggressive tumor biology, this variant may present as a phenotype with no initial benefit and rapid progression. For such rapidly progressive cases, early radiographic reassessment should be performed, and repeat biopsy or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing should be pursued as soon as safely feasible to clarify the resistance mechanism and guide subsequent treatment.

title: EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma featuring massive bronchorrhea, a dominant pulmonary nodule, and migratory ground-glass opacities: a case report and literature review.
authors: Chen L, Yan B, Zheng S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer exhibits profound clinical, radiological, and biological heterogeneity, which poses significant challenges for early recognition and timely diagnosis in select atypical cases. Among rare manifestations, massive bronchorrhea caused by EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma with radiological findings of a dominant pulmonary nodule and migratory ground-glass opacities (GGOs) remains extremely uncommon.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 67-year-old male patient presented with massive bronchorrhea and progressive dyspnea. Serial chest computed tomography (CT) scans revealed bilateral migratory GGOs and a small nodular lesion in the basal segment of the right lower lobe. Empiric antibiotic therapy and subsequent systemic corticosteroid treatment failed to alleviate his respiratory symptoms. Ultimately, markedly elevated sputum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, combined with pathological results from transbronchial biopsy of the right lung nodule, confirmed a diagnosis of EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma. Treatment with osimertinib achieved rapid resolution of bronchorrhea, accompanied by complete regression of the pulmonary nodule and GGOs during clinical follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for lung adenocarcinoma in patients with persistent unexplained bronchorrhea. For patients harboring EGFR-sensitive mutations, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) remain the first-line treatment, yielding favorable therapeutic effects on bronchorrhea control and improving survival outcomes.

title: Disparities in Treatment Patterns for Advanced ALK- and EGFR-Mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients in Mexico.
authors: Sanchez Trujillo LA, Díaz García DA, García-Appendini IC et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lung cancer remains a significant global health burden, with most cases in Mexico diagnosed at advanced stages. Disparities in access to molecular testing and targeted therapies for ALK- and EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may impact patient outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a descriptive, observational, cross-sectional study using real-world data from the Oncology Dynamics database. Mexican patients with advanced/metastatic ALK+ or EGFR+ NSCLC were stratified by healthcare sector (public vs. private) to assess differences in diagnostic testing and treatment access.
RESULTS: Among 324 patients with advanced NSCLC, 63.6% were male and 63.9% were treated in public healthcare settings. EGFR and ALK testing rates were higher in the private sector. EGFR mutations were detected in 47% and ALK rearrangements in 13%. Private sector ALK+ patients all received second-generation inhibitors, while public sector patients received a mix of second-generation (38.5%), first-generation (23.1%), and chemotherapy (23.1%). EGFR+ patients in private care had greater access to third-generation therapies (45.5%) compared to public care (28.2%), where first-generation drugs were most common (62.8%). Supportive care was more frequent in private settings. Significant disparities in molecular testing, targeted therapy access, and supportive care were observed between sectors.
CONCLUSION: This study highlights important differences in molecular testing and access to targeted therapies between public and private healthcare funding sources among patients with EGFR- or ALK-positive advanced NSCLC in Mexico, emphasizing the need for policy interventions to improve equity in cancer care.

title: Patterns of Treatment and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy: A Global, Multicenter, Retrospective Study.
authors: Lin SH, Okishio K, Mizutani H et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
PURPOSE: We report clinical outcomes, mutation testing patterns, and treatment patterns from a global, real-world, retrospective, observational study in patients with stage 1/2 epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
METHODS AND MATERIALS: Data were extracted from medical records of adults with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC (diagnosed January 2016-December 2019), who underwent stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as standard of care. The primary objective was assessment of real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary objectives included assessment of mutation testing patterns, treatment sequencing post-SBRT, real-world time to next treatment or death (rwTTNTD), and real-world overall survival (rwOS).
RESULTS: Data were extracted from medical records of 82 patients across six countries; 66% of patients had medically inoperable tumors; 43% had tumors harboring exon 19 deletion (Ex19del), 55% had L858R, 1% had both Ex19del and L858R, and 1% had L858R and an exon 20 insertion. Overall, 91% of patients had stage 1A/1B disease and 9% had stage 2A/2B. All patients underwent SBRT as standard of care; 31 patients (38%) progressed following SBRT. Of patients who received subsequent treatment (n = 25), most received EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs; 88%; n = 22/25); first-/second-generation EGFR-TKIs n=17, third-generation EGFR-TKIs n=5. Median (95% confidence interval [CI]) rwPFS, rwTTNTD, and rwOS were 47.1 (38.7-57.8), 49.8 (40.7-not estimable [NE]), and 62.9 (50.8-NE) months, respectively. The rwPFS rates at 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 months (95% CI) were 90% (81-95), 76% (65-84), 65% (53-74), 48% (35-60), and 34% (19-48), respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: In this global, real-world, retrospective study in patients with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC who underwent SBRT, the majority of whom had medically inoperable tumors, the 4-year rwPFS rate was <50%. Further studies are needed to confirm the potential role for EGFR-TKI therapy in this setting.

title: Pterostilbene enhances Osimertinib sensitivity in non-small cell lung cancer through FGFR4-dependent ferroptosis.
authors: Wang L, Chen X
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Osimertinib is a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has become a mainstay treatment for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, acquired resistance develops in most patients and ultimately compromises durable clinical benefit. Therefore, effective combination strategies to enhance Osimertinib sensitivity and delay or overcome resistance remain an urgent unmet clinical need.
METHODS: The antitumor effects of pterostilbene in combination with Osimertinib were evaluated in EGFR-mutant and osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cell lines using CCK-8, colony formation, EdU incorporation, wound healing, and Transwell invasion assays. In vivo efficacy and safety were evaluated in nude mouse xenograft models. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, ferroptosis-related biochemical parameters, protein expression profiles, and transcriptomic profiles were analyzed. The involvement of ferroptosis and FGFR4 signaling was further validated using the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) and FGFR4 siRNA-mediated knockdown.
RESULTS: Pterostilbene markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of Osimertinib in vitro and in vivo and restored drug responsiveness in Osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cells. Mechanistically, the combination induced ferroptosis, as indicated by enhanced lipid peroxidation, intracellular Fe2+ accumulation, and reduced expression of key ferroptosis-protective proteins, including GPX4 and xCT. Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis attenuated the antitumor effects of the combination. Furthermore, combined treatment modulated FGFR4-associated ERK/AKT signaling and disrupted redox and iron homeostasis. FGFR4 depletion significantly attenuated ferroptosis induction and reduced the synergistic anticancer effects of the combination, whereas FGFR4 re-expression restored treatment responsiveness, supporting an FGFR4-dependent therapeutic response.
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that pterostilbene enhances the antitumor efficacy of Osimertinib through the induction of FGFR4-dependent ferroptosis, providing mechanistic insights and suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy to overcome EGFR-TKI resistance in NSCLC.

title: Molecular subtyping of brain metastasis-related genes in lung adenocarcinoma via scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq integration: A focus on TPX2.
authors: Xiao G, Ning J, Wen S et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Brain metastasis (BrM) is a common complication of advanced lung cancer with extremely poor prognosis. This study aimed to establish a molecular classification system for stratifying non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)-BrM patients and predicting survival, and to identify key BrM-related molecules and elucidate their mechanisms as potential therapeutic targets.
METHODS: We integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data to construct molecular subtyping models for predicting lung cancer prognosis and immune microenvironment, and to screen key molecules driving BrM. Based on H1299 and PC9-BrM cells, in vitro experiments demonstrated the regulatory role and mechanism of targeting protein for Xklp2 (TPX2) in lung cancer BrM.
RESULTS: We identified 20 BrM-associated genes. Consensus clustering based on these genes stratified patients into two subtypes, with patients in Subtype 2 showing significantly worse overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and disease-specific survival (DSS). Mechanistic analyses revealed marked activation of proliferation-related pathways in Subtype 2. TPX2 was identified as a critical mediator, with significantly elevated expression in BrM lesions compared with primary lung cancer lesions, and TPX2 overexpression correlated with poorer prognosis. Functional assays in H1299 and PC9-BrM cells demonstrated that TPX2 knockdown markedly impaired proliferation, clonogenicity, migration, and invasion. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses and Western blotting validation further indicated that TPX2 likely promotes NSCLC-BrM by activating c-MYC and the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study established a molecular classification system that effectively stratifies NSCLC-BrM patients and predicts survival. Moreover, TPX2 promotes NSCLC-BrM through c-MYC/EMT regulation, offering new insights for targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Expert recommendations on the management of major and minor toxicities associated with the use of lorlatinib in Latin America.
authors: Corrales L, de Carvalho Calabrich AF, Perfetti AA et al.
abstract: Lorlatinib is a third-generation anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)/ROS1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) that has been shown to have high efficacy in the first line setting for treatment of advanced ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, some adverse events have been described that require proper follow-up and management to obtain the maximum benefit from treatment and minimize risk to the patient. These include dyslipidemia and weight gain, conditions that in Latin America have a high prevalence in the general population, which coupled with limitations in timely access to specialized care, could influence both manifestation and management. The objective of this consensus is to provide recommendations tailored to our real-world setting that will optimize the monitoring and early management of toxicities in patients treated with lorlatinib in Latin America.

title: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy in Lung Cancer: Evaluating the Performance of a Cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence Algorithm for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in Chest Radiographs.
authors: Mehrabi M, Askari M
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains a major global health challenge, and early diagnosis critically improves outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to enhance diagnostic accuracy in medical imaging, particularly for thoracic diseases.
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated a cutting-edge AI algorithm for detecting pulmonary nodules in chest radiographs to improve early lung cancer diagnosis.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: In this analytical and experimental investigation, two datasets were used: Group1 (112120 frontal-view chest radiographs labeled for 14 thoracic diseases, including nodules) and Group2 (800 radiographs evenly split into positive and negative cases, with expert consensus labeling). The proprietary AI algorithm is based on CheXNet, a 121-layer convolutional neural network pretrained on ImageNet to initialize weights, enabling transfer learning for superior feature extraction. This model was chosen for its validated performance in thoracic disease detection, particularly in chest X-ray analysis. The datasets were divided into Type A (combining Group1 and Group2) and Type B (using only Group2) to assess performance under different conditions. A five-fold cross-validation was employed.
RESULTS: The model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.73 for Type A and 0.782 for Type B. Sensitivity and specificity metrics were 0.736 and 0.592 for Type A, and 0.716 and 0.734 for Type B, respectively. Notably, the algorithm outperformed radiologists in some cases, demonstrating its capability to detect subtle or challenging nodules.
CONCLUSION: This AI algorithm shows promise as a clinical decision support tool, especially where access to experienced radiologists is limited. Further research is needed to refine the algorithm and validate use in real-world clinical workflows.

title: Feasibility and safety of a 4-week AB-free kava intervention among adults who smoke cigarettes and its effects on reducing lung cancer risk biomarkers: a pilot trial.
authors: Freeman B, Bou Malham M, Hashemian T et al.
abstract: Because of the high prevalence of lung cancer, its poor clinical prognosis, and cigarette smoke being the dominant cause, preventive agents are urgently needed to help reduce lung cancer risk among those with tobacco exposure. Motivated by epidemiological observation, pre-clinical data, and pilot single-arm trial results, AB-free kava (a kava formular of consistent kavalactone composition and free of potentially hepatotoxic flavokavains A and B) may safely prevent cigarette smoke-induced lung cancer. The objective of this study was to evaluate a 4-week AB-free kava intervention among adult smokers for its feasibility, safety, and effects on lung cancer risk biomarkers (urinary 3-methyladenine (3-mA), total nicotine equivalent (TNE)-corrected 3-mA, and plasma 1-(3-pyridyl)-1,4-butanediol (PBD)) via a pilot randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Data were collected during (Week 0, 1, 2, and 4) and after (Week 8 and 12) AB-free kava intervention with nineteen eligible participants enrolled and analyzed (10 in the placebo arm and 9 in the AB-free kava arm). Two participants in the placebo arm experienced liver enzyme elevations, with no elevation observed in the AB-free kava arm. More adverse events (self-addressed) were observed in the placebo arm than in the AB-free kava arm. AB-free kava intervention significantly reduced TNE-corrected 3-mA and showed the trends to reduce urinary 3-mA and plasma PBD. The trial results thus support the feasibility and safety of the 4-week AB-free kava intervention among adults who smoke and preliminarily reveal its efficacy in reducing lung cancer risk, which requires further validation.

title: Effect of pulmonary rehabilitation exercise on postoperative quality of life and symptom cluster in patients with lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Chen Y, Yuan X, Xie Y et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of pulmonary rehabilitation exercise on postoperative quality of life (QoL) and symptom cluster (pain, fatigue, shortness of breath) in lung cancer survivors, meanwhile, to explore the interrelationships among these symptoms.
METHODS: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were retrieved from six databases. Pooled standardized mean difference (SMD) was calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup analyses stratified by intervention duration, multiple sensitivity tests and trim-and-fill analysis were performed. Study-level correlation and regression analyses investigated symptom associations. Evidence certainty was assessed via GRADE.
RESULTS: Ten RCTs with 852 participants were included. Perioperative pulmonary rehabilitation modestly improved QoL (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.91; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23 to 1.58), 6-minute walk distance (SMD = 0.21; 95% CI 0.00 to 0.43) and full vital capacity (SMD = 1.16; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.89), and alleviated the postoperative symptom cluster (pain (SMD = -0.49; 95% CI -0.92 to -0.07), fatigue (SMD = -0.65; 95% CI -0.87 to -0.42) and shortness of breath (SMD = -0.71; 95% CI -1.10 to -0.32)). Moderate-to-strong positive pairwise correlations were detected among symptoms, with pain identified as the core correlated symptom within the symptom cluster.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative pulmonary rehabilitation may improve functional recovery and relieve postoperative symptoms in lung cancer patients. Preoperative intervention and structured rehabilitation lasting at least two months are worthy of attention. As substantial heterogeneity and limited evidence certainty exist, conclusions should be interpreted cautiously. Large standardized RCTs are required to confirm optimal rehabilitation protocols.

title: Endobronchial Pulmonary Actinomycosis With Concomitant Tuberculosis Resembling Lung Malignancy on Presentation: A Case Report.
authors: Bogati S, Pradhan B, Thapa S et al.
abstract: Pulmonary actinomycosis is a rare, indolent infection accounting for roughly 15% of actinomycosis cases, frequently misdiagnosed as tuberculosis or malignancy owing to nonspecific clinical and radiological features. We report a 68-year-old male smoker with chronic alcohol use who presented with acute-on-chronic dyspnea, cough, and fever. Imaging revealed cavitary lesions, consolidation, ground-glass opacities, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy suggestive of tuberculosis or malignancy. Sputum and initial microbiological workup for tuberculosis were largely negative, though a low-level bronchoalveolar lavage GeneXpert signal prompted empirical anti-tubercular therapy. Bronchoscopy revealed an endobronchial mass, and biopsy demonstrated pathognomonic sulfur granules composed of PAS-positive filamentous organisms, confirming actinomycosis with no malignant cells. The patient was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate alongside continued anti-tubercular therapy, with symptomatic improvement. This case highlights actinomycosis as a condition requiring a high index of suspicion when mimicking tuberculosis and lung cancer, reinforcing the necessity of histopathological confirmation for accurate diagnosis and guiding prolonged, appropriate antimicrobial management.

title: Age-related effects of comprehensive in-patient physiotherapy after lung cancer surgery across age groups: an ambispective observational cohort study in middle-aged and older patients.
authors: Manzak Dursun AS, Cinar B, Gökdemir F et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative recovery after lung cancer surgery may be influenced by age, comorbidity burden, and perioperative rehabilitation strategies. However, evidence regarding the age-related effects of structured early inpatient physiotherapy programs remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the age-related effects of a comprehensive in patient physiotherapy (CIPT) program on hospital length of stay (LoS), clinical parameters, symptom-related outcomes, and inflammatory biomarkers in patients undergoing lung cancer surgery.
METHODS: This ambispective observational cohort study included patients who underwent lung cancer surgery and received a structured CIPT program during the postoperative inpatient period as part of standard postoperative care. Participants were categorized into middle-aged and older groups. Outcomes included hospital LoS, clinical parameters (blood pressure, resting heart rate, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate), symptom-related outcomes (dyspnea and fatigue with Modified Borg Scale, and incisional pain with Visual analog scale), and inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein (CRP), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and albumin). Pre- and post-program changes within groups and differences between age groups were analyzed.
RESULTS: Median LoS was 7 [5-10] days in the middle-aged group and 7 [6-10] days in the older group, with no significant difference between groups. Significant improvements in resting heart rate, oxygen saturation, and dyspnea were observed in the older group, whereas dyspnea, fatigue, and incisional pain improved significantly in the middle-aged group. No significant differences were detected between age groups in clinical parameters or symptom-related outcomes. CRP and NLR levels decreased significantly in both groups, while albumin showed a non-significant upward trend over time. Despite a higher comorbidity burden in the older group, no adverse events or clinical instability were observed during the rehabilitation program.
CONCLUSION: The CIPT program appears to be safe and feasible for both middle-aged and older patients following lung cancer surgery. Similar outcomes between age groups suggest that age alone may not represent a barrier to participation in structured early inpatient rehabilitation programs. Early physiotherapy integrated into postoperative care pathways may facilitate recovery without increasing hospital length of stay across age groups, which may also help reduce the potential economic burden associated with prolonged hospitalization.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07441863. First submitted on 17 February 2026 and first posted on 02 March 2026 retrospectively registered.

title: Neurological syndrome with CSF anti-Hu positivity during serplulimab therapy in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: a case report.
authors: Wang L, Zhao Y, Fan B et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved outcomes in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), but neurological immune-related adverse events (n-irAEs) can be severe and disabling. Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is also strongly associated with anti-Hu-associated paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNSs). Neurological syndromes emerging or worsening after ICI exposure may therefore represent post-ICI PNS, in which paraneoplastic autoimmunity and ICI-related neurotoxicity overlap clinically.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 52-year-old woman with stage IV ES-SCLC received four cycles of serplulimab plus etoposide and carboplatin, followed by five cycles of serplulimab maintenance. During maintenance therapy, she developed anorexia, weight loss, and alternating constipation and diarrhea, followed by progressive memory impairment, somnolence, cognitive dysfunction, and gait instability. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed mild mononuclear pleocytosis, and CSF anti-Hu antibody was detected by a cell-based assay at a titer of 1:100; no residual specimen was available for independent confirmatory testing. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated newly developed bilateral paramedian thalamic abnormalities, whereas diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient mapping showed no evidence of acute cerebral infarction. The neurological presentation was classified as an intermediate-risk phenotype under the 2021 PNS-Care criteria. If the reported CSF anti-Hu result is accepted, the recalculated PNS-Care score would be 9, corresponding to the definite PNS category, although interpretation is limited by the absence of orthogonal antibody confirmation. Serplulimab was permanently discontinued, and corticosteroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), followed by individualized IVIG maintenance, resulted in substantial but incomplete neurological recovery. MoCA, MMSE, and mRS improved from 11/30, 12/30, and 3 to 24/30, 22/30, and 2, respectively, although residual cognitive impairment persisted. Separately, a complete response was first documented on July 20, 2021, and radiological CR remained confirmed through May 2023, with no subsequently documented clinical tumor progression before death in January 2025. In 2024, intestinal pseudo-obstruction required segmental colectomy, and histopathology demonstrated lymphocytic inflammation surrounding the myenteric plexus.
CONCLUSION: This case illustrates the diagnostic overlap between paraneoplastic neurological autoimmunity and ICI-related neurological toxicity in a patient with CSF anti-Hu positivity. The later gastrointestinal episode raised the possibility of enteric nervous system involvement, but its etiology remained uncertain.

title: Tumor microenvironment features of CLDN18.2-positive gastric cancer and advances in targeted and immunotherapy.
authors: Tan Y, Cui Y
abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a tight junction protein expressed predominantly in differentiated epithelial cells of the normal gastric mucosa. Changes in cell polarity and junctional organization during malignant transformation can make its epitopes more accessible to antibodies. The tumor microenvironment of CLDN18.2-positive gastric cancer is heterogeneous. Some cohorts show increased CD8-positive T-cell infiltration alongside stromal remodeling and immunosuppressive signals. Interpretation of immunotherapy outcomes also requires consideration of the programmed death-ligand 1 combined positive score, microsatellite instability, and other molecular and spatial immune features. Zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy improved survival in randomized phase III trials enrolling eligible patients with CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Evidence for other treatments is at different stages: satri-cel is supported by a randomized phase II trial, while bispecific antibodies and antibody-drug conjugates have also shown antitumor activity in humans. This review relates target distribution, effector cell function, and stromal and metabolic suppression to the mechanisms of these treatment classes. It examines resistance mechanisms, predictive biomarkers, and treatment selection for patients who meet multiple biomarker criteria.

title: The synthetic biology frontier: engineered oncolytic viruses and viral vectors for next-generation cancer therapy and gene delivery.
authors: Alsharedeh RH, Aljabali AAA, Obeid MA et al.
abstract: Viruses are no longer used merely as naturally occurring tools for gene transfer or as blunt cytolytic agents. Researchers are rewriting their genomes, capsids, tropisms, regulatory elements, and payloads to create therapeutic systems that sense disease, execute conditional programs, and remodel pathological tissue. In oncology, engineered oncolytic viruses (OVs) can combine tumor-selective replication with immunogenic cell death, antigen release, and local immune stimulation. In parallel, viral-vector engineering, particularly AAV and LVs, is addressing central limitations of gene delivery: the prevalence of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies, the difficulty of systemic administration and repeat dosing (AAV), and the manufacturing bottleneck of ex vivo cell therapies (LV). The clinical record is encouraging but uneven: T-VEC has shown that an engineered herpes simplex virus can improve durable responses in selected melanoma lesions, while G47Δ/teserpaturev and newer armed HSV platforms provide evidence of feasibility, safety, and occasional durable responses in difficult solid tumors. Lentiviral vector-based in vivo CAR-T cell generation, exemplified by KLN-1010/inMMyCAR and related first-in-human programs, signals a paradigm shift away from ex vivo manufacturing. However, the broader field has not converted its large preclinical literature into a proportional number of clinically meaningful, systemically deployable medicines. The main bottlenecks remain delivery, tumor heterogeneity, immune clearance, suboptimal pharmacodynamic biomarkers, manufacturing complexity, resistance, and the difficulty of proving benefit for products with delayed or immunologically mediated effects. This review examines the synthetic biology toolkit for programmable viral therapeutics through a unified engineering framework that integrates OVs, AAV, and LVs by design principle rather than by vector class. We discuss tumor-selective promoters, microRNA detargeting, retargeted capsids and ligands, attenuation, genome-scale assembly, immune-stimulatory payloads, bispecific and trispecific engagers, logic-gated circuits, safety switches, serodivergent AAV capsids, biomimetic cloaking, cell carriers, biomaterial delivery systems, and in vivo CAR-T generation. Our central thesis is that the next generation of viral medicines will be selected not by the most elaborate genome, but by the most coherent alignment of five measurable success factors: tumor selectivity, immune remodeling, delivery and biodistribution, controllable safety, and manufacturability. The emerging paradigm is therefore programmable viral therapeutics: context-sensitive biological medicines designed to operate within the constraints of human tumors and human immunity.

title: A patient-derived bladder cancer organoid and xenograft platform for personalized drug response prediction and salvage therapeutics screening.
authors: Lu J, Jie K, Liu C et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Therapeutic resistance remains a major challenge in bladder cancer treatment. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a bladder cancer patient-derived organoid (PDO)-based platform for treatment response prediction and individualized salvage therapy screening.
METHODS: A total of 101 patients with bladder cancer were enrolled to establish 75 PDO lines. The optimal culture medium was determined by transcriptome analysis. Consistency validation was performed via histopathology, immunohistochemistry, whole-exome sequencing, and transcriptomic profiling. A three-step high-throughput screening pipeline for 288 approved agents was developed to identify salvage therapies for patients who were multidrug-resistant, which was validated in patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. A suspension coculture system was constructed to evaluate HER2-targeted chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell cytotoxicity and activation.
RESULTS: FGF4 supplementation significantly enhanced the 3D growth and establishment efficiency of PDOs, yielding a biobank of 75 bladder cancer PDOs. These PDOs faithfully recapitulated the multidimensional features of parental tumors, and showed preliminary concordance with observed clinical treatment responses (cisplatin, gemcitabine, and epirubicin). To address drug resistance, the high-throughput drug screening pipeline maps individualized sensitivity profiles in four cases. In a patient who was multidrug-resistant, idarubicin was pinpointed as a potent candidate agent, with efficacy confirmed in PDX models. To extend the screening platform beyond chemotherapeutics and cover cellular immunotherapies, we verified that the coculture system enabled HER2 expression-dependent CAR-T cytotoxicity evaluation.
CONCLUSIONS: This integrated bladder cancer PDO platform provides a clinically relevant individualized tool for treatment response prediction and individualized salvage therapy selection, particularly for patients with multidrug-resistant disease. Its application may support tailored therapeutic decision-making across chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and cellular immunotherapy.

title: EZH2 at the epigenetic-immune interface: a dual-axis framework for tumor immune evasion and precision combination immunotherapy.
authors: Bai Y, Chen H, Gu Y
abstract: Despite the transformative activity of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and adoptive cellular therapies in selected malignancies, durable responses remain limited in many solid tumors, in part because tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental epigenetic programs can restrict immune recognition and antitumor effector function. Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a catalytic subunit of polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), contributes to this regulation through canonical H3K27 trimethylation-dependent repression, as well as context-dependent functions that extend beyond a simple model of uniform immune suppression. We organize the available evidence into a dual-axis framework in which tumor-intrinsic EZH2/PRC2 activity can regulate major histocompatibility complex class I and II antigen presentation, interferon and viral-mimicry programs, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and T helper 1 (TH1)-type chemokines, whereas tumor-extrinsic EZH2 activity influences macrophages, regulatory T cells, CD8+ T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. Importantly, these effects are not uniformly immunostimulatory: systemic or prolonged EZH2 perturbation has also been associated with myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) expansion in selected preclinical settings. Early-phase human studies established the feasibility, but not the incremental clinical benefit, of combining tazemetostat with programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/PD-L1 blockade or chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy; its subsequent withdrawal after a hematologic safety signal leaves further clinical testing of this strategy to other EZH2- or EZH1/EZH2-directed agents. These observations support mechanism-matched, biomarker-informed, compartment-aware, and temporally controlled EZH2 modulation rather than indiscriminate systemic EZH2 inhibition as the more appropriate framework for future immunotherapy combinations.

title: Efficacy of allogeneic B7-H3 CAR γδ T cells with comparative target assessment across preclinical models in glioblastoma.
authors: Lee S, Park SA, Jo H et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive primary brain malignancy, remains a lethal disease with limited therapeutic progress despite multimodal treatment. Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown promise in several solid tumors, its broader application in glioblastoma is limited by manufacturing hurdles of autologous T cells and the lack of validated tumor-specific antigens. As an alternative, gamma-delta (γδ) T cells have emerged as an attractive cellular platform, offering MHC-independent tumor recognition, robust ex vivo expansion, and suitability for allogeneic use. However, studies applying CAR engineering to γδ T cells in glioblastoma are extremely limited, and an optimal target antigen has not been clearly defined. In this context, our study identified B7-H3 as a clinically relevant target and demonstrated that B7-H3 CAR γδ T cells exhibited superior antitumor efficacy compared to unmodified γδ T cells across patient-derived and orthotopic glioblastoma models.
METHODS: To identify an optimal antigen for γδ CAR-T therapy in glioblastoma, we compared the expression and clinical relevance of HER2, GD2, and B7-H3 through analyses of transcriptomic datasets and patient tumor samples. Based on this, human γδ T cells from healthy donors were expanded ex vivo, engineered with a B7-H3-specific CAR, and evaluated for antitumor activity across patient-derived glioblastoma cell lines, organoids, and orthotopic xenograft models.
RESULTS: B7-H3 was identified as the most clinically relevant antigen, showing high expression in glioblastoma and correlated with poor prognosis and immunosuppressive gene signatures. B7-H3 CAR γδ T cells demonstrated potent cytotoxicity and enhanced cytokine production in B7-H3-high patient-derived glioblastoma models. In patient-derived organoids, CAR γδ T cells significantly reduced tumor viability and invasion. In orthotopic xenografts, a single intracranial administration induced tumor control and prolonged survival, with long-term survivors observed only in the CAR γδ T cell treated group. Across all preclinical models, B7-H3 CAR γδ T cells exerted superior antitumor efficacy compared with parental γδ T cells.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest B7-H3 as a clinically meaningful and therapeutically targetable antigen in glioblastoma and demonstrate the potent preclinical efficacy of allogeneic B7-H3 CAR γδ T cells, supporting their development as a novel immunotherapeutic strategy for glioblastoma.

title: Next-generation CAR-NK therapies: molecular engineering strategies for solid tumors.
authors: Kim ME, Lim Y, Lee JS
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphocytes that exert cytotoxic activity against malignant and virus-infected cells without prior antigen sensitization. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered NK (CAR-NK) cells combine CAR-dependent tumor-antigen recognition with endogenous NK-cell receptor-dependent cytotoxicity against stress-induced ligands and tumor cells with reduced HLA class I expression. Clinical studies of allogeneic CD19 CAR-NK cells have reported antitumor responses without notable cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, or graft-versus-host disease. CAR-NK cells also support allogeneic manufacturing for off-the-shelf cellular therapy. NK-associated intracellular domains including DAP10, DAP12, 2B4, and CD3ζ, cytokine expression using IL-15 or IL-21, and gene editing of inhibitory molecules have been incorporated into CAR-NK designs. PI3K-AKT-mTORC1 and JAK-STAT signaling, glycolytic metabolism, mitochondrial activity, and transcriptional control contribute to CAR-NK cytotoxic function. Recent CAR-NK studies have also examined inhibitory-receptor editing, chemokine receptor expression, and metabolic engineering to improve cytotoxic activity, intratumoral infiltration, and resistance to hypoxia and immunosuppressive signaling in solid tumors. This review examines the molecular mechanisms involved in NK-cell activation and metabolism and evaluates molecular engineering strategies for next-generation CAR-NK therapy in solid tumors.

title: OVM-200, a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine, breaks immune tolerance to survivin in patients with advanced solid tumours: a multicentre, open-label, dose-expansion, phase 1 study
summary: Survivin (BIRC5) is broadly overexpressed in human cancers but, as a self-antigen, is subject to immune tolerance that limits spontaneous antitumour immunity. OVM-200 is a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine spanning full-length survivin, with cathepsin S-cleavable linker sequences inserted between adjacent peptides to enhance antigen processing and presentation. OVM-200-100 was a multicentre, open-label phase 1 study conducted at 4 UK sites. The pooled 2,000-g cohort comprised 27 patients with advanced non-small cell lung, ovarian or prostate cancer, including 24 patients from phase 1b and 3 treated at this dose in phase 1a. OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 3 initial vaccinations, with up to 8 additional doses in patients deriving clinical benefit. The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, secondary endpoints included survivin-specific immunogenicity, and antitumour activity by RECIST v1.1 was exploratory. OVM-200-related adverse events were exclusively grade 1-2, with no treatment-related grade [≥]3 adverse events, dose-limiting toxicities, serious adverse events or deaths. A systematic literature analysis showed low spontaneous anti-survivin seroreactivity in patients with cancer. In our cohort, pretreatment tumours expressed survivin despite low baseline survivin-specific immunity. OVM-200 vaccination subsequently induced robust humoral and cellular responses, with median anti-survivin IgG titres increasing from 20 at baseline to a peak of 81,920 and median interferon-{gamma} ELISpot responses increasing from 16.7 to 504.6 spot-forming units per 10 PBMCs. Patients receiving [≥]4 vaccinations developed higher anti-survivin antibody titres and stronger T cell responses than those receiving fewer doses. Among 24 RECIST-evaluable patients, the best overall response was stable disease (SD) in 6 patients (25%). Patients with SD had significantly higher anti-survivin antibody titres than those with progressive disease (PD) (p=0.0418

title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
summary: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. title: Development of a Thyroid Cancer to Lung Metastasis-on-a-Chip Model
summary: Background: Study of the metastatic cascade in differentiated non-medullary thyroid cancer (NMTC) is hampered by the relative lack of preclinical models that metastasize from primary tumors to other organs. We previously identified regulator of calcineurin 1 isoform 4 (RCAN1.4) as a suppressor of NMTC cell growth, invasion, and metastasis using in vitro systems and tail vein injections in immunocompromised mice. We then reported a microfluidic device mimicking the mouse tail vein injection where cancer cells were allowed to flow directly to lung organoid constructs. We now report the development of a full primary tumor to lung metastasis-on-a-chip (MOC) model for TC. Methods: Resin molds for primary and secondary sites connected by a channel were 3D printed and filled with polydimethylsiloxane to create a molded silicone elastomer. The primary site was seeded with an organoid composed of a hyaluronic acid and collagen-based hydrogel into which FTC236 and HTh74 NMTC cells with and without knockdown of RCAN1.4 were engrafted. The secondary site consisted of a hydrogel organoid into which bronchial epithelial cells and lung fibroblasts were seeded. Culture media was circulated and movement of NMTC cells to the secondary site was assessed. Results: Both cell lines that expressed RCAN 1.4 metastasized to the secondary lung site. RCAN1.4-reduced FTC236 cells had increased metastatic behavior vs controls while HTh74 was less affected by RCAN1.4 loss, similar to prior studies. title: Complete Metabolic Remission With Dose Frequency-Modified Tepotinib Following Capmatinib Intolerance in MET Exon 14-Mutated Non-small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC): A Case Report.
authors: Mandal S
abstract: MET exon 14 (METex14) skipping mutations occur in a subset of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases, mostly affecting older patients with multiple comorbidities. Selective MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) capmatinib and tepotinib represent the standard of care; however, real-world management is frequently complicated by agent-specific toxicity and class-effect peripheral edema. Sequential use of MET TKIs following agent-specific intolerance and the feasibility of non-standard tepotinib dosing schedules remain poorly characterized. A 74-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage IVA METex14-mutated lung adenocarcinoma (cT3N3M1a, malignant pleural effusion, KRAS p.G12V co-mutation) received three cycles of first-line pemetrexed plus carboplatin with residual active disease. Capmatinib 200 mg twice daily, initiated as biomarker-directed therapy, was discontinued after 1.5 months due to severe multi-organ toxicity, including grade 3 hyperglycemia, acute kidney injury, elevated pancreatic enzymes, hypercalcemia, and hyponatremia, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status worsening from 2 to 3. Tepotinib 225 mg once daily was initiated with early clinical and biochemical improvement. Grade 3 bilateral pedal edema at two months necessitated stepwise dose-frequency modification of tepotinib together with diuretic therapy. Apparent radiological progression at 10 months was managed as suspected pseudoprogression in view of sustained clinical stability, and therapy was continued. After 13 months of tepotinib therapy, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT) demonstrated complete metabolic remission in February 2024. This case shows that capmatinib intolerance does not prevent the benefit from sequential tepotinib and that adjusting the dose frequency can effectively manage MET inhibitor-associated peripheral edema without compromising oncological outcomes, achieving complete remission in an elderly comorbid patient.

title: Ras signaling in cancer: From molecular mechanisms to next-generation therapeutic inhibitors.
authors: Hossain J, Choudhury D, Bhattacharyya S et al.
abstract: RAS proteins are small GTP-binding molecular switches that integrate extracellular signals from growth factors, cytokines, and hormones to coordinate key cellular processes. RAS signaling is tightly regulated to maintain tissue homeostasis and ensure precise developmental control. However, dysregulation of this pathway-drives oncogenic transformation, tumor progression, and resistance to therapy. Despite decades of intensive investigation, RAS-driven malignancies remain among the most difficult cancers to treat, highlighting the urgent need for updated perspectives that integrate recent mechanistic insights with rapidly advancing therapeutic strategies. Notably, recent breakthroughs-including mutation-specific inhibitors such as KRAS(G12C) inhibitors and emerging agents such as RMC-7977 and RMC-6236 that selectively target the active RAS conformation-have revitalized the field and underscore the importance of a comprehensive and timely review. In this article, we provide an in-depth overview of RAS signaling, beginning with its molecular mechanisms in normal cellular physiology and progressing to its multifaceted roles in cancer initiation, progression, and chemoresistance. We further summarize current advances in the development of direct RAS-targeted therapeutics, with particular emphasis on the emerging pan-RAS (ON) inhibitors RMC-7977 and RMC-6236, and discuss their potential therapeutic implications particularly in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and non-small-cell lung cancer. Finally, we highlight key challenges for translating RAS(ON) inhibition into durable clinical benefit, including patient selection, biomarker development, early detection and mechanistic understanding of resistance, and rational combination strategies. Collectively, advances in mutation-selective and RAS(ON)-directed therapies are transforming RAS from a historically "undruggable" oncogenic driver into an increasingly tractable target in precision oncology.

title: Heterogeneous response and progression patterns during tarlatamab therapy in relapsed small cell lung cancer.
authors: Murata S, Yoshida T, Tateishi A et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tarlatamab has demonstrated activity in relapsed small cell lung cancer (SCLC). However, lesion-level response heterogeneity and organ-specific patterns of progression during tarlatamab therapy remain poorly characterized in clinical practice.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated patients with relapsed SCLC treated with tarlatamab between June 2021 and March 2026. Overall response at the first radiological evaluation and best overall response were assessed according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. Lesion-level response patterns at the first radiological assessment were categorized as responsive, mixed response, stable, or progressive. Progression sites, intracranial lesion changes, and progression-free survival (PFS) were analyzed. Site-specific findings were summarized at the first evaluation and at overall progressive disease (PD).
RESULTS: Twenty-nine patients were included. Mixed response was observed in 11 (37.9%) patients and across the RECIST response categories at the first radiological evaluation. The median PFS was 3.2 months and was longest in the responsive group, intermediate in the mixed-response group, and shortest in the progressive group. Among 15 patients evaluable for intracranial response, seven experienced at least 30% intracranial tumor shrinkage at the first assessment, and four subsequently developed intracranial progression. Among 20 patients with disease progression, 12 had progression at three or more sites. Site-specific assessments showed that decreased or stable disease could coexist with overall PD.
CONCLUSION: Tarlatamab showed heterogeneous response and progression patterns in relapsed SCLC, including frequent mixed response and intracranial progression. Lesion-level assessment may provide a more comprehensive characterization of disease behavior during tarlatamab therapy.

title: Clinical Study on Fuzheng Jiedu Huayu Therapy in Combination With Chemotherapy and Immunotherapy for Improving Survival Rates in Extensive-Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer
summary: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine malignancy. Approximately 70% of patients are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease, and only a subset of patients benefit from immunotherapy. Under the leadership of Academician Sun Yan, the principal investigator, our research group previously relied on the Big Data Platform of the National Cancer Center and undertook major projects including those from the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Beijing Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine for collaborative of major and difficult diseases with integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine, as well as the National Key R\&D Program. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) of 600 cases demonstrated that the traditional Chinese medicine "Fuzheng Jiedu Huayu" (strengthening vital energy, detoxifying, and resolving stasis) combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy synergistically improved progression-free survival and disease control rate in patients with extensive-stage SCLC. Building on this foundation, the current project will enroll 224 patients with extensive-stage SCLC (1:1 ratio). On the basis of first-line treatment with immunotherapy plus platinum-based agents and etoposide, patients will be administered either "Fuzheng Jiedu Huayu" traditional Chinese medicine or a placebo. The study will employ objective response rate, progression-free survival, and overall survival as outcome measures, conducting a multicenter, large-sample RCT. Additionally, a multimodal database of no less than 1000 cases will be established, striving to obtain an IND approval, thereby contributing to the realization of the goal set forth in the "Healthy China 2030" Planning Outline: "By 2030, increase the overall 5-year cancer survival rate by 15%."

title: Testing of Tazemetostat in Combination With Topotecan and Pembrolizumab in Patients With Recurrent Small Cell Lung Cancer
conditions: Extensive Stage Lung Small Cell Carcinoma
Limited Stage Lung Small Cell Carcinoma
Recurrent Extensive Stage Lung Small Cell Carcinoma
summary: This phase I trial tests the safety, side effects, and best dose of tazemetostat in combination with topotecan and pembrolizumab in treating patients with small cell lung cancer that has come back after a period of improvement (recurrent). Tazemetostat may stop the growth of tumor cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth. Chemotherapy drugs, such as topotecan, work in different ways to stop the growth of tumor cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing, or by stopping them from spreading. Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies, such as pembrolizumab, may help the body's immune system attack the cancer, and may interfere with the ability of tumor cells to grow and spread. Giving tazemetostat in combination with topotecan and pembrolizumab may shrink or stabilize recurrent small cell lung cancer.

title: A Trial of Talabostat (BXCL701) and Pembrolizumab in Participants With Metastatic Castrate-Resistant Prostate Cancer (mCRPC) Either Small Cell Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer or Adenocarcinoma Phenotype
summary: An open-label, multicenter, Phase 1b/2 study to identify the recommended Phase 2 dose and assess the efficacy and safety of talabostat administered orally, as monotherapy and in combination with pembrolizumab, in participants with mCRPC. Participants enrolled in the Phase 2a portion of the study will have either SCNC (Cohort A) or adenocarcinoma phenotype (Cohort B), while the Phase 2b randomized portion of the study will enroll only the histologic subtype(s) showing preliminary evidence in Phase 2a. The study will also assess other efficacy parameters, such as radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), prostate-specific antigen progression-free survival (PSA PFS), overall survival (OS), and duration of response (DOR), as well as the safety of the combined treatment.

title: Circulating tumor DNA dynamics and mutational profiles as indicators in neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for resectable or borderline resectable non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Jiang W, Lei S, Liu S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy has reshaped the treatment landscape for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet critical gaps remain in real-time monitoring and personalized adaptation.
METHODS: In this observational study, patients were evaluated via imaging and multidisciplinary review for subsequent surgery or radiotherapy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Serial plasma samples for circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics and mutational analyses were collected. The endpoint was event-free survival (EFS). A pognostic mutational signature was developed using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression.
RESULTS: Among the 138 patients, 46.4% and 52.2% underwent surgery and radiotherapy, respectively. Compared to patients with persistently positive ctDNA, the ctDNA non-shedder exhibited a numerically longer EFS (hazard ratio [HR] 0.26, 95% CI: 0.06-1.25, p = 0.062), and the clearance group exhibited a statistically longer EFS (HR 0.33, 95% CI: 0.11-0.97, p = 0.040). Patients with positive ctDNA before surgery/radiotherapy showed a shorter EFS (HR 3.38, 95% CI: 1.26-9.08, p = 0.010), and positive ctDNA was correlated with a numerically shorter EFS (HR 9.72, 95% CI: 0.98-95.96, p = 0.051) in patients assessed as stable disease (SD) of high heterogeneity in the exploratory subgroup analysis. For patients with post-C1 negative ctDNA, no EFS difference was observed between those receiving 3-4 versus 2 cycles of chemoimmunotherapy (HR 1.54, 95% CI: 0.56-4.26, p = 0.41). For patients with post-C1 positive ctDNA, the post-C1 quantity was associated with clearance (AUC = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.55-0.89, p = 0.019). After balancing clinical characteristics, LASSO-Cox regression selected four genes (SLX4, IRF4, TP53, and SOX2) to construct a prognostic signature for EFS. The AUC at 36 months was 0.75, 0.71, 0.74 in the training, validation and full cohort. The high-risk group demonstrated a shorter EFS (p = 0.0002).
CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal ctDNA assessment identified high-risk subgroups in neoadjuvant NSCLC, particularly by refining prognosis in heterogeneous SD populations. An exploratory gene-based mutational signature provided potential molecular risk stratification.

title: A Study of LY4336619 in Adult Participants With Advanced Solid Tumors
summary: The main purpose of this study is to evaluate how safe and effective LY4336619 is in adults with advanced cancer. Some participants will receive LY4336619 alone, and some will receive it with another cancer medicine. Participants will be in the study for up to 2 years, depending on how they tolerate and respond to treatment.

title: LDCT Screening Cost-Effectiveness for Familial Lung Cancer Risk in Taiwan.
authors: Hsieh FC, Liu CH, Shi HY
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Most economic evaluations of low-dose CT (LDCT) screening focus on heavy smokers, with limited evidence for individuals with a family history of lung cancer (LCFH). This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of LDCT screening for individuals with LCFH using Taiwan epidemiologic data and cost data derived from the Taiwan National Health Insurance program.
STUDY DESIGN: A Markov model simulation evaluated the cost-effectiveness of LDCT screening vs nonscreening using 10,000 iterations in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis, a 1-year cycle, a 20-year time horizon, and a 3% annual discount rate.
METHODS: The analysis adopted the perspective of the Taiwan health care payer and assumed annual LDCT screening with full adherence. The willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold was set at $32,440, corresponding to Taiwan's 2024 gross domestic product per capita. We used incremental costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) to calculate the incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR). Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate parameter uncertainty.
RESULTS: At the specified WTP threshold, LDCT screening yielded an ICUR of $23,786/QALYs, which was below the prespecified WTP threshold. In the simulated cohort, 158,375 LDCT examinations resulted in 609 lung cancer diagnoses over 20 years. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated a 61.22% probability of cost-effectiveness. Results were most sensitive to lung cancer incidence in the nonscreening cohort, LDCT positivity rate, and positive predictive value.
CONCLUSIONS: LDCT screening for individuals with LCFH was cost-effective at the selected threshold under modeled assumptions. Targeted implementation in high-risk populations may enhance value-based resource allocation; however, real-world adherence, evolving treatment costs, and program scalability should be considered in coverage and reimbursement decisions.

title: Low-Dose CT Lung-RADS 2022 for the Management of Screening- and Non-Screening-detected Lung Cancer Associated with Cystic Airspaces.
authors: Mascalchi M, Cavigli E, Puliti D et al.
abstract: Background Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (CA) can be misinterpreted as a benign lesion, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis; however, the effect of the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) 2022 criteria remains unverified. Purpose To retrospectively determine the frequency and outcomes of lung cancer associated with CA during screening and explore the potential effect of Lung-RADS 2022 on earlier diagnosis. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis included participants with lung cancers from three trials: the National Lung Screening Trial (2002-2007); Italian Lung Cancer Screening Trial, or ITALUNG (2004-2010); and German Lung Cancer Screening Intervention trial, or LUSI (2007-2016). Two radiologists jointly reviewed low-dose CT images to identify and morphologically characterize lung cancer associated with CA. Associations with histologic features, stage, and other variables were assessed. Lung cancer-specific survival was analyzed using Fine-Gray regression accounting for the competing risk of non-lung cancer death. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, stage, detection status, and trial. Lung-RADS 2022 criteria for atypical pulmonary cysts were applied. Results Seventy-three cancers associated with CA were identified in 1258 participants (median age, 64 years [IQR, 61-69 years]; 43 male), including 44 of 716 (6.1%) screening-detected and 29 of 542 (5.4%) non-screening-detected cancers. Multilocular morphologic type was associated with a more advanced stage than unilocular morphologic type (12 of 24 vs 15 of 49; P = .02). The 5-year lung cancer-specific survival was 51.4% (95% CI: 39.3, 62.3) for cancers associated with CA and 53.2% (95% CI: 50.1, 56.2) for 1054 participants with noncystic non-small cell lung cancer. No evidence of a difference in survival was observed (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.15 [95% CI: 0.81, 1.63]; P = .44), and results remained consistent in multivariable models. Lung-RADS 2022 might have enabled earlier diagnosis in 55 of 73 cancers associated with CA (75%). Conclusion Lung cancer associated with CA accounted for 6.1% of screening-detected and 5.4% of non-screening-detected lung cancers. Outcomes were similar to those of noncystic non-small cell lung cancer, and Lung-RADS 2022 may facilitate earlier diagnosis. Clinical trial registration nos.
