title: Lymphedema as an initial manifestation of paraneoplastic rheumatic syndromes: a case series of six patients.
authors: Zhang GH, Zhang LL, Jiang MN et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Lymphedema as the initial symptom poses significant challenges in the early diagnosis of underlying malignancies masquerading as rheumatic diseases.
METHODS: This study retrospectively analyzed six patients who were hospitalized at Beijing Shijitan Hospital between October 2015 and October 2025 with paraneoplastic rheumatic syndromes (PRS) presenting with lymphedema as the initial manifestation. Data on clinical manifestation, laboratory and imaging findings, diagnoses, treatments, and prognosis were collected.
RESULTS: Six patients (3 males, 3 females; median age 66 years) presented with lymphedema as the initial manifestation of PRS. The initial rheumatologic diagnoses were leukocytoclastic vasculitis (n=2), undifferentiated connective tissue disease (n=2), Sjögren's syndrome (n=1), and anti-synthetase syndrome (n=1). The median interval from lymphedema onset to rheumatic diagnosis was 5.5 months. All patients received glucocorticoids, and four received immunosuppressants; none achieved durable benefit. The median interval from rheumatic diagnosis to therapy failure was 1 month, and from therapy failure to cancer diagnosis was 1 month. The underlying malignancies included lymphoma (n=3), lung adenocarcinoma (n=2), and gastric adenocarcinoma (n=1). During a follow-up of 1 to 13 months, two patients showed significant improvement in lymphedema, whereas the remaining four died.
CONCLUSION: Malignancies may present with lymphedema as the initial symptom, mimicking rheumatic diseases. Underlying malignancy should be highly suspected, particularly when there is a poor response to immunosuppressive therapy. Early recognition and screening for malignancies are crucial for improving patient outcomes.

title: Healthcare Staff Perspectives on Improving Access to and Receipt of Lung Cancer Screening.
authors: Nguyen KV, Narendra J, Strahley A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer screening (LCS) rates remain disproportionately low compared with screening rates for other cancers, especially among marginalized populations. Improving uptake is challenging due to multilevel barriers involving the healthcare system, clinical environments, and interest holders. Although prior research has examined barriers from the perspectives of patients and healthcare providers, there is a paucity of research identifying LCS barriers from the perspective of healthcare staff (e.g., nurses) who help carry out screening processes.
OBJECTIVE: To understand multilevel barriers to equitable LCS access and receipt from the perspectives of healthcare staff.
DESIGN: This was a qualitative study of 15 semi-structured interviews. Participants were US healthcare staff members (e.g., nurses or medical assistants). Participants completed virtual semi-structured interviews eliciting their perspectives of LCS barriers across each level of the Health Equity Implementation Framework (HEIF), a framework for assessing determinants of equitable LCS implementation across multiple levels (e.g., patient, provider, clinical encounter, and inner/outer healthcare system contexts). Interview transcripts were analyzed using template analysis and a combined deductive-inductive qualitative approach. KEY RESULTS : Most healthcare staff had little clinical knowledge about LCS but agreed that LCS has benefits for early detection. Participants identified barriers to equitable LCS across each HEIF level, such as patient concerns related to claustrophobia, limited provider time to discuss LCS, patient and provider LCS unawareness, inadequate media coverage, and limited transportation options. Participants also described provider bias or discrimination, smoking-related stigma, healthcare mistrust, cost concerns, and societal disregard for older, under-resourced, and/or marginalized populations as barriers affecting equity in LCS uptake. Several identified that barriers were interconnected and spanned multiple HEIF levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Healthcare staff uniquely described barriers to LCS across all levels of the HEIF. Multilevel interventions, especially those aimed at higher HEIF levels, may reduce LCS barriers and inequity.

title: Lung cancer detection beyond screening eligibility through an incidental lung nodule program.
authors: Wang HY, Lo Cascio C, Qi J et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lung cancer screening has improved early detection among individuals who meet established age and smoking criteria. However, many patients who develop lung cancer remain ineligible for screening. Incidental pulmonary nodules (ILN) identified on imaging performed for other indications may provide important complementary pathway for early lung cancer detection, but the contribution of structured ILN programs to cancer detection outside conventional screening eligibility remains incompletely characterized.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected data from two urban academic hospitals from January 2023 through January 4, 2026. Patients with ILN requiring surveillance were identified using natural language processing of radiology reports and navigator review. Screening eligibility was classified according to 2021 United States Preventive Services Task Force criteria. Cancer detection, stage, histology, treatment, and factors associated with cancer among screening-ineligible patients were evaluated.
RESULTS: Among 2,804 patients requiring follow-up, 2,248 (80.2 %) were screening ineligible, 466 (16.6 %) eligible, and 90 (3.2 %) unclassified. Lung cancer was diagnosed in 73 patients (2.6 %), including 44 (60.3 %) who were screening ineligible. Of these, 15 were never-smokers and 29 were former or current smokers who did not meet screening criteria. Thirty-six (81.8 %) had stage 0-II disease, 21 (47.7 %) underwent definitive surgical resection, and 36 (81.8 %) had adenocarcinoma. Nodule diameter > 8 mm was associated with lung cancer diagnosis (adjusted odds ratio 15.89; 95 % CI 5.24-71.47).
CONCLUSIONS: The ILN program identified substantial early-stage, clinically actionable lung cancers among patients outside conventional screening eligibility. The high proportion of early-stage diagnoses and definitive resections supports ILN programs as a complementary pathway to organized lung cancer screening.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid-derived small extracellular vesicles reveal a compartment-specific diagnostic signature for NSCLC leptomeningeal metastasis.
authors: Kuang PP, Li YS, Hu T et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a devastating complication of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet timely diagnosis remains challenging because conventional approaches, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology, have limited sensitivity, particularly at initial presentation. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), as nanoscale carriers of protected regulatory cargo, have emerged as promising substrates for liquid biopsy. However, in anatomically compartmentalized central nervous system malignancies, the extent to which disease-associated sEV-miRNA signals are preserved across biofluids remains unclear.
METHODS: We profiled sEV-associated miRNAs by small RNA sequencing in CSF and plasma samples from NSCLC patients with clinically adjudicated LM status (NC, LM-, and LM+), including paired specimens where available. Biofluid-specific miRNA programs were characterized using weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and diagnostic models were developed using machine learning with Random Forest and LASSO-based feature selection. Model performance was evaluated in an independent validation cohort relative to final adjudicated LM status and compared with initial and cumulative MRI and CSF cytology assessments.
RESULTS: CSF-derived sEV-associated miRNAs showed markedly stronger disease-stratification capacity than plasma-derived signals (ARI = 0.813 vs. 0.255; cluster purity = 0.868 vs. 0.694), revealing profound biofluid asymmetry. Network analysis identified a dominant LM-associated module in CSF (r = 0.74, P = 9 × 10⁻⁷) with limited preservation in plasma, indicating that LM-related vesicle-associated molecular programs are compartment-restricted. From this CSF-specific nanoscale vesicle signature, we derived a four-miRNA diagnostic panel comprising hsa-let-7e-5p, hsa-miR-30d-5p, hsa-miR-486-5p, and hsa-miR-375. In the independent validation cohort, the single-sample sEV-miRNA panel achieved an AUC of 0.935, with 86.4% sensitivity and 87.5% specificity. By comparison, initial MRI and initial CSF cytology showed sensitivities of 50.0% and 77.3%, respectively, whereas cumulative MRI and cumulative CSF cytology showed sensitivities of 70.0% and 86.4%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: CSF-derived sEV-associated miRNAs encode an LM-proximal molecular program that is not faithfully captured in plasma, underscoring the importance of biofluid compartmentalization in nanobiotechnology-based biomarker discovery. Our findings establish a compartment-aware sEV-miRNA diagnostic strategy for accurate LM detection and provide a conceptual framework for extracellular vesicle-based molecular diagnostics in central nervous system malignancies.

title: Single-port thoracoscopic complex vs simple lung segmentectomy: Comparative outcomes and feasibility.
authors: Liu H, Han B, Pei Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Complex lung segmentectomy, although effective for early-stage lung cancer, is less widely adopted because of its technical complexity.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to compare perioperative outcomes, quality of life (QoL), and survival between complex and simple lung segmentectomy performed using single-port thoracoscopy to determine its clinical feasibility.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This retrospective analysis screened 218 patients; after exclusions, 210 patients underwent complex (n = 100) or simple (n = 110) segmentectomy at Zhanjiang Central Hospital. Propensity score matching resulted in 92 patients per group. Single-port thoracoscopic surgery was performed, and perioperative outcomes, complications, QoL assessed using the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and survival evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves were analyzed. Statistical analyses were performed using t-tests, χ2 tests, and log-rank tests (p < 0.05).
RESULTS: Complex segmentectomy was associated with longer operative time, greater postoperative drainage, and longer hospital stays (p < 0.001). Cough (60.87% vs 32.61%; p = 0.007) and air leakage (54.35% vs 19.57%; p < 0.001) were more common in the complex group. No significant differences were observed in postoperative lung function, other complications, such as infection or arrhythmia, or QoL at 6 months (p = 0.071). Survival curves showed comparable prognosis (p = 0.860).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite increased perioperative demands, complex lung segmentectomy achieves lung function, QoL, and survival outcomes similar to those of simple segmentectomy, supporting its role in the treatment of early-stage lung cancer. These findings support its broader application in specialized settings and may inform optimized surgical approaches.

title: The CD39/CD73 adenosinergic pathway is increased by proinflammatory states and modified by chemo-radiation in human non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Ashley K, Ding A, Arammash M et al.
abstract: Recent clinical trials show prominent anti-tumor activity of CD73-blocking antibodies in combination with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) antagonists in a subset of patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which highlights the need to understand the properties of the CD39/CD73 pathway in human lung malignancies and its modulation by other anti-cancer therapies. To address this, we study the distribution, biological context, spatial heterogeneity, clinical significance, and modulation of CD39/CD73 using multiplexed quantitative immunofluorescence and spatial transcriptomics analysis of multiple NSCLC patient cohorts, as well as in vitro experiments of cultured NSCLC cells. Our results reveal an asymmetric distribution of the CD39/CD73 pathway within the tumor microenvironment, preferential expression in lung adenocarcinomas with elevated PD-L1 and effector T cell infiltration or lacking STK11/KEAP1 mutations, limited intratumor spatial heterogeneity, and differential modulation of cancer cell CD73 by proinflammatory cytokines and systemic radio-chemotherapy. Collectively, our results can inform optimal design of therapeutic interventions and patient selection strategies.

title: CT referrals and cancer detection in patients referred by general practitioners with non-specific symptoms and signs of cancer: A retrospective study.
authors: Ohana NL, Axelsen J, Wilkinson MS et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In Denmark, since 2011-2012, a national cancer patient pathway (CPP) has been in place for patients presenting with non-specific signs or symptoms of and signs of cancer (NSSC). Many cancer patients initially do not display organ-specific alarm symptoms when examined by general practitioners (GPs).
PURPOSE: To characterize referral symptoms in patients undergoing contrast-enhanced CT chest-abdomen-pelvis (TAP) for non-specific signs of cancer or vague symptoms, in relation to radiological findings and final diagnoses. Second, the study assessed diagnostic accuracy of CT TAP for detecting malignancy in these patient groups.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included all patients referred by GPs to CT TAP at Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark through NSSC or vague cancer symptoms from May to August 2024. Referral symptoms and radiology reports were compared to final clinical diagnosis at the end of NSSC-CPP.
RESULTS: The study included 725 patients. The most frequent referral symptoms were weight loss (51.3%), pain (45.0%), and fatigue (39.4%). CT TAP reports indicated that 20.6% of cases had findings suggestive of cancer, most commonly lung cancer. Overall, 9.2% received a malignant diagnosis, most commonly lymphoma or lung, pancreatic, and colorectal cancer, while 11.3% received a benign diagnosis. Cancer was rare in patients with vague symptoms.
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that CT TAP is a valuable tool for diagnosing patients with non-specific signs or symptoms of cancer in general practice. These findings support the continued use of CT TAP within the cancer pathway as an important tool for identifying patients who need further investigation.

title: Occult lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed by EBUS-TBNA after pneumothorax resolution in an RA-ILD patient with respiratory failure.
authors: Zhu C, Gu Y, Liu Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: RA-ILD is a serious complication of RA. Patients are prone to spontaneous pneumothorax and have a higher risk of lung cancer.Given poor lung function and high risk of pneumothorax recurrence, conventional biopsy is challenging, making diagnosis difficult.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 67-year-old male with a history of smoking and well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis presented with chest tightness and pleuritic chest pain. On admission, he was found to have respiratory failure (PaO₂ 58.9mmHg). Chest CT revealed left-sided pneumothorax with interstitial lung disease.Following closed thoracic drainage, the pneumothorax resolved, which was confirmed by follow-up chest X-ray.But the persistence of the patient's chest pain despite resolution of the pneumothorax prompted further investigation.CT pulmonary angiography identified a suspicious mass in the left lower lobe with adjacent rib destruction and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Given the high risk of recurrent pneumothorax from percutaneous biopsy in a patient with recent pneumothorax and pre-existing respiratory failure, a multidisciplinary team recommended Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration(EBUS-TBNA) as a safer alternative. EBUS of enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes (stations 7 and 11L) confirmed poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma.The patient subsequently received first-line chemotherapy with pemetrexed, cisplatin, and bevacizumab, after which his condition gradually stabilized.
CONCLUSION: Both pneumothorax and interstitial lung disease can mask an occult malignancy, underscoring the need for clinical vigilance. EBUS-TBNA is a safe and effective diagnostic option in such high-risk cases.

title: Assessing the suitability of Australian regulatory asbestos monitoring methods for naturally occurring asbestos in high-dust mining environments.
authors: Thelan V, Liebenberg A
abstract: This review provides an integrated evaluation of current asbestos sampling and analytical methodologies to determine if these are appropriate for assessing exposure to naturally occurring asbestos (NOA), particularly in the high-dust environments associated with Western Australian mining operations. Asbestos exposure remains a significant occupational health concern globally, with strong evidence linking fiber inhalation to serious diseases including mesothelioma and lung cancer. Although the commercial use of asbestos has been banned in Australia since 2003, mining activities continue to intersect with geological formations that may contain NOA minerals, creating ongoing potential for occupational exposure. For occupational hygienists working in these settings, this raises a practical question: when a worker's personal air sample is collected and analyzed using standard regulatory methods, does the result reliably reflect their actual exposure to potentially hazardous fibers? The answer to this question has direct implications for risk assessment, exposure controls, and health surveillance decisions made at the operational level. Current regulatory monitoring in Australia relies primarily on the Membrane Filter Method (MFM), a morphology-based analytical approach originally developed for environments dominated by asbestos fibers, rather than the complex mixed dust conditions typical of mining operations. Known limitations of this method include reduced fiber visibility under high particulate loading and delays between sample collection and reporting of results. Critically, samples collected during the highest-dust activities, and therefore the periods of greatest potential worker exposure, are precisely those most likely to be voided due to particulate overload. This review critically evaluates the scientific, regulatory, and geological factors relevant to NOA exposure assessment in mining settings, including the relationship between fiber characteristics and disease, international developments in monitoring methodologies, and the geological occurrence of NOA in Western Australia. The findings highlight the need to reassess current monitoring practices and may inform occupational hygiene practice, regulatory decision-making, and future research directions in industries where NOA may be encountered.

title: Rare paraneoplastic syndromes associated with thymoma: case reports and literature review.
authors: Jia W, Jin L, Li X et al.
abstract: Thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal tumor, which is linked to the loss of self-tolerance and the presence of autoimmunity. Various interactions between thymoma and autoimmune diseases have been identified, including myasthenia gravis, systemic lupus erythematosus, pure red cell aplasia, and pemphigus. In this retrospective case series, we reported rare autoimmune disorders with different organ involvement associated with thymoma. These included ocular paraneoplastic pemphigus, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, diffuse panbronchiolitis and myositis. Our series broadens the spectrum of autoimmune disorders with shared T cell-mediated and B cell-dependent pathogenesis, underscoring the recurrence or relapse of thymoma-associated autoimmunity. The recognition of rare autoimmune presentations charts future treatment decisions and multidisciplinary care.

title: Application of weighted gene co-expression network analysis to explore the targets of treadmill training in rats with spinal cord injury.
authors: Zhang H, Guo M, Meng L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spinal cord injury (SCI) describes any damage to the spinal cord that results in a loss of function. With these injuries being commonly treated with subsequent treadmill training (TM), this study aimed to reveal the mechanisms facilitating TM-mediated rehabilitation following a SCI.
METHODS: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and then subjected to a weighted gene co-expression network analysis to identify TM-associated modules. Co-expression network construction, functional annotation, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, and transcription factor (TF)-miRNA-target regulatory network were then conducted. We established an SCI rat model and validated key RNAs using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Predicted interactions between miR-135a-5p and JAK2 and STAT1 were tested using dual-luciferase reporter assay.
RESULTS: Total 640 and 877 genes separately differentially expressed in SCI 8d + TM vs. SCI 8d and SCI 14d + TM vs. SCI 14d comparison groups were screened and merged as the DEGs, which were further narrowed to four TM-associated modules linked to the glutamatergic synapse and ribosome biogenesis pathways. PPI network evaluations identified v-Akt murine thymoma viral oncogene homolog 1 (AKT1), Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) as hub nodes. JAK2 and STAT1 were also shown to have interactions in module b. TF-miRNA-target regulatory network revealed that both STAT1 and JAK2 were targets of miR-135a. RT-qPCR results confirmed upregulation of AKT1 and STAT1 and downregulation of JAK2, TNF and miR-135a after TM. Dual-luciferase reporter assays revealed the direct binding of miR-135a-5p to JAK2 and STAT1.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that TM facilitates SCI recovery by regulating AKT1, JAK2, TNF, STAT1 and miR-135a.

title: Association of serum Sema4D and ANGPTL4 levels with disease severity and prognosis in myasthenia gravis patients.
authors: Li W, Zhang M, Wang Z et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the relationship of serum semaphorin 4D (Sema4D) and angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) levels with disease severity and prognosis in anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive myasthenia gravis (MG) patients.
METHODS: Between December 2023 and April 2025, 468 anti-AChR antibody-positive MG patients hospitalized at our center were prospectively enrolled and divided into good- and poor-prognosis groups according to whether they achieved minimal manifestations (MM) or better status at the 1-year follow-up. Healthy controls were also enrolled. Serum Sema4D and ANGPTL4 levels were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Correlations were evaluated by Spearman's rank correlation. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors for poor prognosis. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the predictive value of the two biomarkers alone and in combination, and clinical and combined models were developed to evaluate the biomarkers' incremental predictive value.
RESULTS: Serum Sema4D and ANGPTL4 levels were significantly higher in MG patients than in healthy controls (both p < 0.001). Compared with the good-prognosis group, the poor-prognosis group had higher proportions of Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) class IV-V, dysphagia, and thymoma, and higher Myasthenia Gravis Quality of Life 15-item revised (MG-QoL15r) and Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) scores (all p < 0.05), and significantly higher levels of both biomarkers (both p < 0.05). Both Sema4D and ANGPTL4 correlated positively with MG-QoL15r and CONUT scores and with each other (r = 0.431, p < 0.001). Multivariable logistic regression showed that MGFA class IV-V, dysphagia, thymoma, higher MG-QoL15r and CONUT scores, and elevated serum Sema4D and ANGPTL4 levels were all independent risk factors for poor prognosis (all p < 0.05). The combination of the two biomarkers yielded an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.841, superior to either marker alone. Adding the biomarkers to the clinical model significantly improved prognostic discrimination, with the AUC increasing from 0.874 to 0.907 (p = 0.0002).
CONCLUSION: Combined measurement of serum Sema4D and ANGPTL4 is associated with disease severity and poor prognosis in anti-AChR antibody-positive MG and shows good predictive value for patient prognosis.

title: Antigen-presenting-cell-associated programs in thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis: public transcriptomic reanalysis and archived cell-model observations.
authors: Lu C, Chai Y, Wang Y et al.
abstract: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis (TAMG) involves a complex thymic immune environment, but tissue antigen-presenting-cell (APC) programs do not by themselves establish a soluble-signal mechanism. We re-analyzed public single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data and examined archived records from one Thy0517 AB-thymoma line and a THP-1-derived dendritic cell-like preparation. Donor-resolved single-cell summaries showed antigen-presentation-associated expression across several APC compartments, whereas IL21 transcripts were sparse and most evident in Tfh-like CD4+T cells. IL21R/IL2RG-containing modules were exploratory tissue annotations, not validation of IL-21R signaling in the culture model. In two TAMG sections, unadjusted APC antigen-presentation and maturation/costimulation correlations attenuated after covariate adjustment; associations with migratory DC, Tfh/IL-21 and GC-like B-cell programs differed between sections. A single normal adult thymus sample provided a descriptive, unmatched reference. The retained morphology and CD11c panels document induction of the THP-1-derived preparation, not an effect of subsequent Thy0517 conditioning. A separate cytokine worksheet contained IL-21- and IL-6-labeled entries, but concentration units and calibration could not be verified. Unverified quantitative marker endpoints were removed. Representative CD4+T-cell plots document the assay format only and do not establish frequency or ratio changes. These observations provide descriptive human tissue context and archived cell-model documentation; they do not establish a Thy0517-conditioning effect or an IL-21-specific TAMG mechanism.

title: Dual CD40/CD28 co-stimulation reprograms the solid-tumor microenvironment to unleash CAR-T and endogenous anti-tumor immunity
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, owing to poor T-cell persistence, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and cancer immune evasion. Here we describe LACO-Stim (lymphocytes-APC co-stimulator), a chimeric co-stimulatory molecule composed of an agonistic anti-CD40 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) and the CD28 intracellular signaling domain, such that a single molecule activates CD40-expressing antigen-presenting cells while delivering CD28 co-stimulation to the T cell that bears it. Co-expressed with a 4-1BB-based CAR (LACO-CAR-T), it enhanced anti-tumor activity in vitro and achieved durable, complete in most mice, tumor regression rather than transient control in xenograft and immunocompetent models. In immunocompetent hosts, LACO-CAR-T activated dendritic cells, reprogrammed tumor macrophages toward M1-like, antigen-presenting states, and induced epitope spreading with endogenous CD8 T-cell responses against tumor neoantigens. Single-cell transcriptomics and RNA-velocity analysis revealed coordinated immune remodeling: T cells shifted toward a more stem-like, less terminally exhausted state, regulatory T cells declined in frequency and suppressive function, and myeloid cells acquired antigen-presentation programs while excessive inflammatory and suppressive signaling was restrained. LACO-Stim further synergized with anti-PD-1 blockade to control tumor growth. LACO-Stim thus enables CAR-T cells to coordinate intrinsic T-cell reinforcement with extrinsic immune reprogramming, converting an immunosuppressive TME into a de-inflamed (reduced inflammatory signaling), de-suppressed rather than merely armed niche that supports endogenous anti-tumor immunity.

title: IL13 critically contributes to the antitumor activity of polyfunctional CD4+ T cells driven by constitutively active Stat5
summary: The presence of polyfunctional T cells capable of concurrently producing multiple cytokines correlates with favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cancer. We previously reported that overexpression of constitutively active Stat5a (CASTAT5) confers polyfunctionality on tumor-specific CD4 T cells, enabling durable antitumor immunity following adoptive cell therapy. However, the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor effects of CASTAT5-modified T cells remain unclear. Here, we identify interleukin-13 (IL13) as a critical effector cytokine contributing to the multifaceted antitumor activity of CASTAT5-conditioned polyfunctional CD4 T cells (C5-CD4). C5-CD4 T cells exhibit a prominent T helper 2 (Th2) cytokine profile, accompanied by extensive epigenomic remodeling at the Th2 cytokine loci, as revealed by Hi-C and histone-modification CUT&Tag assays. Neutralization of IL13 diminished the antitumor efficacy of C5-CD4 T cells. Furthermore, targeted Il13 disruption substantially impaired tumor control and was associated with reduced donor T cell expansion and persistence, diminished systemic cytokine and chemokine responses, and attenuated activation of endogenous tumor-reactive CD8 T cells. Nonetheless, IL13 overexpression alone in donor CD4 T cells failed to fully recapitulate the therapeutic activity of C5-CD4 T cells, indicating that IL13 is a critical contributor but is insufficient to account for the full antitumor activity conferred by CASTAT5. Single-cell RNA sequencing associated donor-derived IL13 with increased representation of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells and IL13-signaling in monocytes and macrophages exhibiting tissue-repair-associated transcriptional programs. Moreover, Il13 disruption diminished the therapeutic efficacy of CASTAT5-expressing CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in a mouse B-cell lymphoma model. Reanalysis of a human CD19CAR-T infusion-product dataset further revealed an association between IL13 expression and type 2 cytokine signatures
